What was actually solved

A true GTO solve of 50-ante deep heads-up poker is not possible on a PC — it is a problem the size of a national lab. What this is instead is an abstracted equilibrium: the game is simplified in two specific, disclosed ways, that simplified game is solved properly, and real hands are mapped onto it.

Preflop: nothing is simplified

All 630 combinations collapse to 81 strategically identical starting hands, because before a board exists the four suits are interchangeable. That collapse is exact, so preflop is solved with no card abstraction at all.

Postflop: hands are bucketed

Similar hands are grouped. Grouping is potential-aware: two hands only share a bucket if they have a similar spread of outcomes across future cards, not merely the same equity today.

Bet sizes are restricted

Preflop: limp, min-raise, 50% pot, 100% pot, jam. Postflop: 25%, 50%, 100%, 150% pot, jam. Max 4 bets per street.

Nine stack depths

10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50, 65, 80 and 100 antes, solved separately. The top-up and rathole rules keep every real stack inside that range.

Why bucketing is not optional

People ask why this is not done like PioSOLVER, which uses every combination with no grouping at all. The answer is storage. Pio solves one flop against one pair of ranges. A bot has to know every board. Card-perfect postflop play for a single stack depth works out at roughly:

573 flop classes × ~100,000 decision points × 630 combos ≈ 140 GB

Per stack depth. Your browser is not downloading that. Bucketing brings it to tens of megabytes, and that is the entire reason it exists.

How honest is the result?

Strong, and principled, and beatable by an expert who finds the seams between buckets. It is labelled an approximation everywhere in this app because that is what it is. What it is not is a set of hand-written rules pretending to be a solver.

Run the solver yourself

The solver source lives in solver/ in this repo. It is written in Rust for speed. You need it only if you want to re-run or change the solve — playing the bot needs nothing installed.

  1. Install Rust once (Windows PowerShell):
    winget install Rustlang.Rustup
    then close and reopen PowerShell. Nothing else is needed — the project pins a toolchain that does not require Visual Studio.
  2. Go to the solver folder:
    cd C:\Claude\Code\shortdeck\solver
  3. Build and run:
    cargo run --release
  4. It writes ..\data\strategy.json and ..\data\strategy.bin. Commit and push those two and the website picks them up.

Useful switches:

  • --iters 100000000 — how many hands to learn from, per stack depth. More is better and slower; it is the main quality dial.
  • --depths 50 — solve one stack depth only, for a quick test.
  • --dump-states 4000 — regenerate the file that proves the website's hand-grouping matches the solver's.

All nine depths run at once, one CPU core each. Roughly 300,000 hands per depth take 14 seconds on an 8-core machine, and it scales linearly from there — so 20 million takes about 15 minutes and a billion takes about half a day.

How to actually play this game

Every number on this page was computed by exhaustive enumeration of the 36-card deck, not estimated. The preflop hand ranking uses Monte Carlo simulation.

1. The one thing to understand: equities run close

Take out the 2s through 5s and every hand gets better. But your opponent's hand gets better too, and it gets better by roughly the same amount. The result is that the gap between a great hand and a mediocre hand shrinks.

What this means at the table: pushing a small preflop edge all-in is worth much less than in holdem. AA versus KK pays you 74.6% instead of 81%. QQ is an actual underdog to AK. Because nothing dominates, post-flop skill and position matter more, and pre-flop all-in gambling matters less.

2. The rule of 3 and 6 (not 2 and 4)

In holdem after the flop there are 47 cards you have not seen, so each out is worth about 1/47 = 2.1% per card. Multiply outs by 2 for one card, by 4 for two cards.

In short deck there are only 31 unseen cards after the flop (36 minus your 2 minus the 3 on the board). Each out is worth 1/31 = 3.2% per card. So:

Rule of 3

One card to come (turn to river): outs × 3. With 30 unseen it is actually 3.3% per out, so this slightly under-counts — which is the safe direction.

Rule of 6

Two cards to come (flop to river): outs × 6. Accurate up to about 6 outs, then it starts to over-count. See the table.

Where the rule of 6 breaks: it is good to about 6 outs and then drifts high, the same way the rule of 4 does in holdem but worse. At 8 outs it says 48% and the truth is 45.6%. At 12 outs it says 72% and the truth is 63.2%. For big draws, use the rule of 3 twice and subtract a little, or just remember: a big combo draw is around 60-65%, never 70%+.

3. Flush draws are weak. Straight draws are strong.

This is the single biggest adjustment coming from holdem, and it is pure counting.

There are only nine cards in each suit. If you hold two of a suit and two more are on the flop, that is four of the nine accounted for — five left, not nine. Meanwhile an open-ended straight draw still has its full eight outs, because straights depend on ranks and no rank was removed, only whole low ranks.

Practical version: stop paying big prices for flush draws. Start paying them for open-enders. A flush draw in short deck is worth roughly what a gutshot-plus is worth in holdem. And when you DO make a flush, it is close to unbeatable — it beats a full house.

4. Real flop match-ups

All ten spots below were solved exactly — every possible turn and river was enumerated. The first four use the same aces on the same board and change only the draw, so you can see exactly what each type of draw is worth.

5. The 81 starting hands, ranked

Short deck has 630 two-card combinations, but before a board exists the suits are interchangeable, so there are exactly 81 strategically different starting hands (9 pairs, 36 suited, 36 offsuit). Here they are ranked by equity against a random hand.

The pair cliff

This is the most striking thing in the whole ranking. Watch what happens to pocket pairs:

HandRank (of 81) Equity vs random
AA173.0%
KK269.3%
QQ366.4%
JJ463.7%
TT561.3%
992056.3%
884250.0%
776144.5%
667838.9%

The top five pairs occupy the top five slots outright. Then it falls off a cliff: 66 is 78th out of 81 hands. In holdem, 22 keeps value because it can flop a set that nobody sees coming. In short deck, 66 makes the worst set, the worst straight, is dominated by every other pair, and there are only three ranks below the 9 to hide behind. Small pairs are close to unplayable here and that surprises almost everyone.

One honest caveat about this list. "Equity against a random hand" measures raw strength in an all-in, not how playable a hand is. It systematically flatters big offsuit cards and punishes connectors: 76s shows up 79th, but a hand that makes straights and flushes plays far better after the flop than a hand like J6o that can only make one weak pair. Use this table to understand raw equity. Use the solver's actual ranges (GTO Solver tab) to decide what to play.

6. Core principles the solver plays by

Where these come from. The principles below follow directly from the maths on this page — they are not received poker wisdom, and every one of them can be checked against a number above. To see what the solver itself actually does, hand by hand and street by street, use the GTO Solver tab: it lets you walk the solved tree and read the real frequencies.

Play more hands, fold less

Every hand is closer to every other hand. The gap between the best and worst starting hand is far smaller than in holdem, so tight-passive is a losing style here.

Position is worth more

Because equities run close, the hand that acts last wins more of the marginal pots. The button posts the extra ante for exactly this reason.

Respect the flush

Flushes beat full houses and only 480 exist. If a lot of money goes in on a three-suited board, someone has it.

Top pair is a bluff-catcher

Not a value hand. Everyone holds big cards, so everyone pairs big boards. Stacking off with top pair is the classic short deck leak.

Sets are worth a stack

You flop them more often and they hold up more often, because the main thing that beats them - a flush - almost never comes.

Draws are betting hands

An open-ender is often the mathematical favourite against a made overpair. It should be raising, not calling.

The rules of Short Deck

Also called 6+ Hold'em or Six Plus. Same shape as No Limit Hold'em, but four ranks are missing and two hand rankings change because of it.

1. The deck: 36 cards, not 52

Every 2, 3, 4 and 5 is removed. What is left is 6, 7, 8, 9, T, J, Q, K, A in all four suits — nine ranks, 36 cards.

Why this changes everything: you have removed 16 of the 20 lowest cards. Every hand that gets dealt is made of big cards, so everybody connects with the board far more often. Top pair is no longer a strong hand. Two pair is routine. The average winning hand at showdown goes up a full rank compared to holdem.

The Ace is still both high and low

The Ace plays as the card below the 6, so A-6-7-8-9 is a straight — the short deck "wheel". It is the lowest straight, exactly as A-2-3-4-5 is in holdem. That means the Ace is part of two straights (A6789 and TJQKA), same as always.

2. Hand rankings (highest to lowest)

#HandCombos (36 cards) Combos (52 cards)Change
1Straight flush2440same
2Four of a kind288624same
3Flush4805,108MOVED UP
4Full house1,7283,744MOVED DOWN
5Straight6,12010,200same
6Three of a kind16,12854,912same
7Two pair36,288123,552same
8One pair193,5361,098,240same
9High card122,4001,302,540same

Combos = how many distinct 5-card hands of that type exist. Rarer beats more common. These are exact counts from full enumeration of all 376,992 five-card short deck hands, not estimates.

Why a flush beats a full house here

There are only nine cards of each suit instead of thirteen. Making five of them becomes hard: flushes fall from 5,108 combos to just 480. Full houses only fall from 3,744 to 1,728. So the flush flips from being roughly 1.4× more common than a boat to being 3.6× rarer — and the ranking follows the rarity.

Why a straight still beats trips

This is the one people argue about, and the maths settles it. Yes, straights get easier to make relative to holdem — but trips get harder faster. Straights drop from 10,200 to 6,120 combos (down 40%). Trips drop from 54,912 to 16,128 (down 71%). Trips remain 2.6× more common than straights, so the straight stays above it.

Some older home games rank trips above straights. This trainer does not, and that is the correct Triton-style ruleset. If trips beat straights, open-ended straight draws become close to worthless and the whole game distorts.

A quirk nobody re-ranks

Look at the bottom of the table: high card (122,400) is actually rarer than one pair (193,536) in short deck. By pure frequency logic, high card "should" beat a pair. No game does this — it would be unplayable — but it tells you something useful: an unpaired, undrawing hand in short deck is close to worthless. You will be paired or better most of the time just by accident.

3. The betting: antes, not blinds

Short deck is normally an ante game. Instead of two blinds, every player puts in one ante before the cards, and the button puts in an extra one.

Heads-up, as played in this trainer:

  • Both players ante 1A. ("A" = one ante, the unit of money here.)
  • The button posts an extra 1A button ante, so the button is in for 2A total and the opponent for 1A.
  • The starting pot is 3A.
  • Because the button has the biggest forced bet, the button acts last preflop as well as last on every later street. This is the opposite of heads-up holdem, where the button acts first before the flop.
Plain version: the button here works like the big blind and the dealer button combined. It costs more, but it has position on every single street. That is a real edge, and it is why the non-button has to fight so hard preflop.

After that it is standard: flop (3 cards), turn (1 card), river (1 card), no-limit betting on each, best five-card hand wins.

4. Stack rules used in this trainer

  • Everyone starts at 50A.
  • Fall below 10A and you are automatically topped back up to 50A.
  • Rise above 100A and the excess is skimmed off and banked — you keep the money, but you sit back down with 100A.

So live stacks always sit between 10A and 100A. This is deliberate: it means the solver only ever has to know how to play a known, bounded set of stack depths, which is what makes a solved bot possible on a laptop instead of a data centre.

5. Quick differences cheat sheet

Flush draws are weak

Only 5 outs, not 9. There are just nine cards per suit and you can see four of them. A flush draw is now worse than an open-ended straight draw.

Straight draws are strong

Still 8 outs, and every out is worth more because fewer cards remain unseen. Connectors go up in value; suited cards go down.

Top pair is not a made hand

It is a bluff-catcher. Everyone has big cards, so everyone pairs the big board cards.

Sets and straights are the money

You flop a set more often (fewer cards to dodge) and it stays good more often, since flushes are rare.

Aces run worse

AA versus KK is 74.6% here, not 81%. Everything runs closer together, so getting all-in preflop is less profitable than you think.

Rule of 3 and 6, not 2 and 4

With only 31 unseen cards after the flop, each out is worth about 3% per card instead of 2%. See the Strategy tab.
